title: Mother's Maiden Name (Again)
summary: Chapter One, session one. Six volunteers -- any age, any background, all new to the city -- travel in separately, then are processed into civil defence together over one ordinary day: a medical, a kit issue, an errand into the city, a canteen, and a night shift clearing vermin out of a storm drain. Nothing that happens to them today is dangerous, and two things that happen to them today are the whole campaign.
structure: Four quarters, many short scenes rather than four long ones. The morning is warm and administrative and is shaped like a school day -- an assembly, then two periods with a kit queue between them -- because this is a school and the mecha campaign is happening around a timetable. The afternoon takes them into the city and puts them in a room with the most important stranger in the campaign, the evening is built around one NPC who claims them before anyone else does, and the night is a completely routine SF2E first combat carrying more weight than anything in it looks like it carries.
designRequirement: Give six strangers reasons to act as one unit before anything is at stake. Plant the DNA flag. Put the antagonist in front of them, kind and useful, and let the table draw its own conclusions. Do not explain the Frames, the Watcher, Cicada, the mitflits or the Gap.
castingNote: Taka is built to be immediately likeable and he is doing real structural work later -- warm, funny, claims all six as his table before they can decide where to sit. Play him at full warmth. What the table makes of him is theirs.
downtime: None. One continuous day of intake -- the four-slice economy is taught next session, when there is something worth spending a slice on.

scenes.title: From Up Here
scenes.description: Scene 0. The GM's opening speech over one picture of the world and the city: the rift at Kortos, the four who stopped it, the prophecy that named Kurose, the Directorate that built the city, and how the city feels about it. No questions to the table -- that is next scene.

scenes.title: The Road In
scenes.description: The same acceptance letter, six separate journeys. Each player in turn says how their character looks, how we first see them, and one small problem they hit on the way into the city -- then names the skill they used, rolls it, and tells us how it went. Deliberately no shared beat -- they do not meet yet.

scenes.title: Intake Medicals
scenes.description: A queue, a form that asks for mother's maiden name twice, and a two-hundred-year-old doctor telling each of them privately that their blood screen came back irregular and not to worry about it. This is where the six of them are a group for the first time.

scenes.title: Assembly
scenes.description: The whole intake is gathered in the drill hall and addressed by the Deputy Director. This is the session's -- and the campaign's -- one deliberate exposition beat: what this city is, what the Directorate is for, what happened here, and what these students are actually being asked to become. It is also the roster parade: every significant adult in the campaign is on that platform or along that wall, with their rank and department legible, and the party gets one look at all of them before any of them matter. Built with real things to do rather than a monologue -- the speech carries the official version, and the checks carry what the speech leaves out.

scenes.title: School: First Period
scenes.description: An hour after being told what they are, the party has double period one like anybody else. Two rooms at opposite ends of a corridor: the city on a wall map, taught by a man fond of it, or a workshop safety induction run by a woman with horns who is shouting before the last of them is through the door. One optional roll each, and the first checks in the campaign that can cost something.

scenes.title: Kit Issue
scenes.description: A busy quartermaster's counter. Every player picks personnel equipment from a curated Directorate menu, and any player who works Nobu socially can earn one small, unexplained extra -- a plant, not a payoff, for much later. Personnel kit only: vehicles and Frames are Episode Two's business. The Section Officer turns up at the end in person, to inspect what they drew, find fault with it, and hand them the afternoon's errand himself. GM tool: @UUID[Macro.865e0ce3b7d302e5]{Open Equipment Locker} -- opens the real inventory UI, already showing every connected player the same catalogue and budget.

scenes.title: School: Second Period
scenes.description: The last lesson before they are let off campus, and the first hour of the day where an adult is pleased to see them. A room of jars and trays holding thirty years of things caught within a mile of it, or a live telephone exchange where eleven people connect every call on the island and have never once listened to one.

scenes.title: The Errand
scenes.description: A collection run into the city -- the session's only exterior, and the only time all six are outdoors together. The Directorate's docket lists the item under a catalogue name nobody has used in a century, so the task is unfinishable until a retired chemist in a tea house reads it in nine seconds and explains it twice, because he enjoys explaining. He is kind, he is useful, he says one true and unsettling thing about their employer, and he offers them a way to reach him again. The party gets a real, disclosed choice over how to file the win against the man who sent them. Somewhere on the route, a cicada stencil on a wall: unremarked, unexplained, worth nothing today. GM-ONLY: the old man is the campaign's primary antagonist and nothing in the scene may suggest it.

scenes.title: The Tram Back
scenes.description: A short, quiet connective scene -- no NPCs, no mandatory checks -- giving the six of them a few unstructured minutes between The Errand and the canteen's noise.

scenes.title: Canteen
scenes.description: Taka claims all six of them as his table before the plates are cleared, and the wider trainee body gets its first real screen time. The room is a crowd scene and should carry at least three gatherable rumours for social checks. Ends with the Section Officer walking in personally to read Section Nine's assignment out -- last, worst, non-negotiable, storm drain clearance -- and standing there while it lands.

scenes.title: The Walk Down
scenes.description: The session's deliberate relax beat between the canteen's cold ending and the fight -- ten minutes, no NPCs required (Taka may see them off), kitting up and walking to Dock C with nobody else in the room.

scenes.title: Flood Tunnel Clearance
scenes.description: The campaign's first fight. Two quick checks to get the drainage and compactor system running, which is what wakes the six Giant Centipedes nesting in it. An optional closing-in hazard -- the compactor cycle itself -- can run alongside the fight for a harder, more tactical version. The Section Officer is waiting at the top when they come out, to take the report and to make clear what he thought of it. Ends with a long rest back at student accommodation.

requiredBeats: Every one of the six is told privately that their screen flagged, and the party is given every opportunity to work out it was all of them.
Nobody explains what the screen tests for. Shucks is forbidden, and he thinks the rule is stupid.

An old man in a tea house solves a problem the Directorate could not, says one true thing about the Directorate, and leaves the party a way to contact him. Nothing in the scene suggests he is anything other than kind, because in that scene he is nothing other than kind.
The Section Officer is met in person, more than once, and is the one who hands them the night's job himself.
The Deputy Director addresses the intake, and the party hears -- from the top of the organisation, in public -- what the Directorate says it is for and what it says they are for.
Every significant adult in the campaign is visible at the Assembly, with rank and department legible, before any of them becomes important.
The party sits two school periods, each a free choice between two rooms, and comes out of them with something they can use or with extra work that costs them the afternoon or the night.
danglingThreads: What a blood screen with a pre-printed IRREGULAR tick-box is actually looking for.
What the blacked-out paragraph in the founding charter says, and who painted over it.
Who the old man in the tea house is, and why a retired chemist reads a two-century-old catalogue like sheet music.
That trainee messages are read as routine policy, and that the party agreed to it this morning without reading the form.
A cicada, stencilled on a wall in the city, that meant nothing at the time.
The name on the order that assembled them, spoken once from the platform and not explained.
notes:
FOUR STANDING RULES SET BY THIS EPISODE, applied across all content from here on.

1. THE SECTION OFFICER IS A REAL, PRESENT CHARACTER -- "not a voice over a tannoy, but instead a real minor antagonist" (Ingram). He appears in person at the end of Kit Issue to inspect and to hand out the errand, in person at the Canteen to read the storm-drain assignment out himself, and in person at the top of the drain when they come back up. He is the impetus that pushes the party to the next task and the voice that gives feedback on the last one.

2. NEVER PREDICT THE TABLE'S RESPONSE. No line in any file may assert what the table will feel, decide or conclude. State what the SCENE does instead. (Earlier drafts of this episode's structure and casting notes broke this; both were rewritten.)

3. CROWD SCENES CARRY RUMOURS -- at least three, gatherable by social checks. Assembly has its set authored. Canteen does not yet; see that file's meet-someone beat, where the gap is flagged.

4. SESSION LENGTH IS NOT A CONSTRAINT. Sessions are units of content, not units of time. Nothing is cut or compressed to fit a clock.

ASSEMBLY, placed third. Ingram: "I'd like the players to be gathered into an assembly where they will get an exposition dump from the Deputy Director and at this event we can have the players witness lots of these characters and see them for the first time, notice their rank, understand their role and get an early impression of who they are... I noticed a lack of this sort of information in the first session or chapter." Between Intake Medicals and Kit Issue: processed as bodies, addressed as a cohort, equipped as personnel, sent out as a unit. It is deliberately the one place in Chapter One where the world is explained out loud, and it is built so the explaining is not a monologue -- the speech carries the official version, the checks carry what it leaves out.

THE CICADA STENCIL planted on The Errand's route is the earliest seed of the cult: worth nothing at the time, and the same mark that turns up again at the Episode Two manifestation site.

Build history: design/episode-one-redesign.md and bible/LEDGER.md #20.

SCHOOL. Two periods on day one, bracketing kit issue. Four rooms, none of them the same kind of room: the city on a wall map, a workshop safety induction, a natural history collection, and a live telephone exchange. Three rules govern every school period in this campaign and they are not negotiable -- not rolling is free and is a normal thing for a student to do; the risks and rewards are never announced beforehand; and failure costs something real.

THE FAILURE CURRENCY ON DAY ONE IS NOT A QUARTER. The four-quarter day is not named to players until The Board, in Episode Two. First period charges failure against the slack in the afternoon errand -- which is where the tea house, the old man and the cicada stencil all live. Second period is too late in the day for that, so it charges the evening instead and sends them into the flood tunnel Fatigued. By the time The Board explains the time economy, a player who failed here has already felt what losing free time costs, which is the better teaching order.

WHAT THE FOUR ROOMS PAY OUT, NONE OF IT ANNOUNCED. Local studies pays this afternoon on The Errand. The workshop pays tonight in the tunnel and again in next episode's hangar, and its critical success is Brack using the player's name. Natural history pays tonight as a free, already-made Recall Knowledge on the centipedes. Signals pays next episode and changes a scene rather than helping a check -- a player who sat it can hear that the Comms Officer broke procedure to warn them.
